findings.title: Unhealthy flusher processes are never killed (isinstance check never matches SpawnProcess)
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes here are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context; `SpawnProcess` derives directly from `BaseProcess`). The guard is therefore always False in production, so `process.kill()` is never called. Previously `self.process.kill()` was invoked unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher process is detected as hung (`cause = "hang"`), the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second process for the same shards. Two processes then flush and produce the same Redis shards concurrently, which can duplicate/fragment segments on the `buffered-segments` topic, and each restart leaks another process and Redis connection set. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or the concrete `SpawnProcess`) in the isinstance check (the same mistake exists in `join()` at line 346, where `terminate()` is likewise dead code).

findings.title: Added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 does nothing. The comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" is misleading, and the intended synchronization does not happen — the test still relies on timing between `step.poll()` and the background flusher thread, so `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. If a real wait is needed, capture the unpatched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep` at module import, as test_flusher.py does) or poll for the condition with a timeout.

findings.title: Metric tag key inconsistency and high-cardinality shard tag values
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is emitted with tag key `shards` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `shard` for the same value, so dashboards/queries cannot filter uniformly. Additionally, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,4,8,12"`); since the shard→process grouping changes with partition assignment, this produces a combinatorial set of tag values on `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (a per-segment metric), which inflates metric cardinality and breaks continuity with the previously untagged series.

findings.title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard`
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called from anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). It should be removed; leaving it invites a future caller to restart a process by shard id, which would silently restart the whole shard group and overwrite `self.processes`/`self.buffers` entries.

findings.title: Zero assigned shards results in no flusher process at all
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields `num_processes == 0` when `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty (also when `max_processes` is explicitly passed as 0, which the CLI `--flusher-processes 0` allows). In that case `process_to_shards_map` is empty, no process is started, and `submit()` silently never flushes anything while still accepting messages. Guard with `max(1, ...)` / validate the CLI option so a misconfiguration fails loudly instead of running a consumer that writes to Redis but never produces segments.

findings.title: New multi-process test only checks internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that the total count of mapped shards is 4, but never submits spans and never asserts that segments from shards owned by *both* processes are produced. The count assertion also passes for an incorrect mapping (e.g. shard 0 duplicated and shard 3 missing would still total 4) — comparing the union of mapped shards to the assigned shard set would catch that. As written, the multiprocessed flusher path (>1 process actually flushing distinct shards) is untested.
